1. Organization

Kernel → Grid → Blocks → Warps → Threads

When you launch a CUDA kernel, you create a grid of blocks. Each block contains many threads. The GPU internally groups those threads into warps of 32 threads.

my_kernel<<<num_blocks, threads_per_block>>>(...);
Grid is the whole job. Blocks are assigned to SMs. Warps are what the SM schedules. Threads are the logical workers you write code for.
2. Block

What is a block?

A block is a group of CUDA threads that runs on one SM. Threads in the same block can cooperate using shared memory and can synchronize with __syncthreads().

Good to rememberOne block stays on one SM until it finishes.
Example256 threads/block = 8 warps/block.
3. Warp

What is a warp?

A warp is usually 32 threads. It is the basic execution group on NVIDIA GPUs.

Warp = 32 threads
Same instruction
Different data

Example:

x[i] = x[i] + 1;

For one warp, thread 0 updates x[0], thread 1 updates x[1], and so on. They execute the same instruction on different data.

Warp divergence: if 16 threads take the if-branch and 16 take the else-branch, the warp runs both paths serially with different active masks. That wastes lanes and slows things down.
4. Hardware

What is an SM?

An SM, or Streaming Multiprocessor, is the GPU hardware unit that hosts blocks and schedules warps.

Modern SMs often have many CUDA cores/ALU lanes, registers, shared memory, load/store units, and warp schedulers. Exact counts depend on architecture.

A CUDA thread does not permanently own a CUDA core. Warps are dynamically scheduled onto execution units.
5. Scheduling

Block scheduler vs warp scheduler

Block scheduler Assigns blocks from the grid to available SMs. You usually do not choose the exact SM.
Warp scheduler Inside an SM, picks a ready warp and issues that warp’s next instruction. 
Kernel launch
  ↓
Grid of blocks
  ↓ block scheduler
Blocks assigned to SMs
  ↓
Blocks split into warps
  ↓ warp scheduler
Ready warp's next instruction is issued
6. Instructions

Who holds the instructions?

The full kernel instructions live in GPU program/code memory and instruction cache. Each warp has a program counter, or PC, pointing to the warp’s next instruction.

Kernel instruction stream:
Instruction 0: compute index
Instruction 1: load x[i]
Instruction 2: multiply by 2
Instruction 3: store y[i]

Warp PCs:
Warp 0 PC → Instruction 1
Warp 1 PC → Instruction 2
Warp 2 PC → Instruction 1
Warp 3 PC → waiting on memory from Instruction 1
The warp does not hold all instructions. It holds its current position in the instruction stream.
7. Latency hiding

What if one instruction takes multiple cycles?

If a warp issues an instruction that takes many cycles, the scheduler can switch to another ready warp instead of waiting idle.

Cycle 0: issue Warp 0 instruction
Cycle 1: issue Warp 1 instruction
Cycle 2: issue Warp 2 instruction
...
Cycle 10: Warp 0 may be ready again

Latency vs throughput

LatencyHow long until one instruction's result is ready.
ThroughputHow often the pipeline can accept new work.

If every dependent instruction has 10-cycle latency and the scheduler can issue one instruction per cycle, you need roughly 10 ready warps per scheduler to hide that latency. Real GPUs are more complex, but this is the right intuition.

8. Launch configuration

How to choose blocks and threads

Simple 1D default

int threads_per_block = 256;
int num_blocks = (N + threads_per_block - 1) / threads_per_block;

my_kernel<<<num_blocks, threads_per_block>>>(...);

Why 256?

1 warp = 32 threads
256 threads/block = 8 warps/block

Common choices

128 threads/block  = 4 warps
256 threads/block  = 8 warps
512 threads/block  = 16 warps
1024 threads/block = 32 warps

2D data example

dim3 threads(16, 16); // 256 threads

dim3 blocks(
    (width  + 15) / 16,
    (height + 15) / 16
);
Best default: start with 256 threads per block, compute enough blocks to cover the work, then benchmark and tune.
9. Cheat sheet

Final summary

Grid
The whole kernel launch: a collection of blocks.
Block
Group of threads. Assigned to one SM. Can use shared memory and __syncthreads().
Warp
Group of 32 threads. Basic scheduling/execution unit.
Thread
Logical worker with its own registers/data.
SM
Hardware unit that hosts blocks and schedules warps.
Block scheduler
Assigns blocks from the grid to SMs.
Warp scheduler
Picks a ready warp and issues its next instruction.
Program counter
Per-warp pointer to the next instruction.
Scoreboard
Tracks whether a warp’s next instruction can run.
Latency hiding
When one warp waits, the scheduler runs another ready warp.
Occupancy
How many blocks/warps can be resident on an SM.
Warp divergence
Threads in the same warp take different paths, so paths run serially.

Final mental model

Blocks organize work.
Warps execute work.
SMs host the work.
Warp schedulers keep the hardware busy.
